federal_fail_nodes.failure_name: Judicial Reversal / Appeal of Agency Action
federal_fail_nodes.summary_html: A **court reverses or vacates** a CPS or agency decision due to procedural error, insufficient evidence, or constitutional violation. Federal review data (CFSR, ASFA) tracks judicial determinations on reasonable efforts and due process.
federal_fail_nodes.authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — judicial findings of 'reasonable efforts' compliance  
- **CFSR Regulations (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of judicial/agency conformity  
- **42 U.S.C. § 1983** — civil-rights remedy for unconstitutional removals (14th & 4th Amendments).
federal_fail_nodes.failure_basis: Court finds state failed to meet evidentiary or procedural standards; order reversed or vacated.
federal_fail_nodes.corrective_hooks: Remand for compliance; damages under §1983; policy revision via state DSS or court rule.
source_reference: ASFA and CFSR oversight; §1983 judicial remedy

key_cases.case_name: M. L. B. v. S. L. J.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a State may not condition an indigent parent's appeal from a decree terminating parental rights on her ability to prepay record preparation fees.
key_cases.relevance: M.L.B. guarantees that the appellate mechanism for reversing an erroneous termination stays open to parents who cannot pay.
key_cases.quote: Mississippi may not deny M. L. B., because of her poverty, appellate review of the sufficiency of the evidence on which the trial court found her unfit to remain a parent

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before it may terminate parental rights, and reversed New York's fair-preponderance standard.
key_cases.relevance: A termination or dependency order entered on a preponderance standard is constitutionally defective and subject to reversal under Santosky.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.case_name: Croft v. Westmoreland County Children and Youth Services
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court reversed summary judgment for the agency, holding that a caseworker who forced a father from the home on the basis of an uncorroborated anonymous tip, while holding no opinion that abuse had occurred, lacked objectively reasonable grounds and committed an arbitrary abuse of government power.
key_cases.relevance: Croft is the model case for reversal of agency action taken without objectively reasonable grounds.
key_cases.quote: Even considered together, minor inconsistencies which provide no affirmative evidence of sexual abuse cannot alone establish the objectively reasonable grounds necessary to remove a family member from the family unit

key_cases.case_name: Rogers v. County of San Joaquin
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the grant of qualified immunity, holding that chronic medical neglect and unsanitary home conditions did not establish exigency and that the warrantless removal violated clearly established Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights.
key_cases.relevance: A removal order resting on conditions that never amounted to exigency is subject to reversal and § 1983 liability.
key_cases.quote: we hold that it was clearly established that warrantless removal of children is permissible only in cases of exigency

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County, North Carolina
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause does not require appointed counsel for indigent parents in every parental-rights termination proceeding, leaving the appointment decision to the trial court in the first instance subject to appellate review.
key_cases.relevance: A reviewing court assessing reversal for denial of counsel applies Lassiter's case-by-case due process inquiry rather than a per se rule.
key_cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the dismissal, holding that inclusion on New York's Central Register of Child Abuse and Maltreatment, disseminated to prospective child care employers and coupled with a statutory burden on those employers, deprives the listed person of a protected liberty interest, and that the 'some credible evidence' expungement standard creates too high a risk of error to satisfy due process.
key_cases.relevance: Valmonte is the model for judicial invalidation of an agency registry scheme on procedural due process grounds rather than on the facts of the underlying allegation.
key_cases.quote: the dissemination of information from the Central Register to potential child care employers, coupled with the defamatory nature of inclusion on the list, does implicate a liberty interest

federal_fail_nodes.summary_html: A **child is removed without exigency or warrant**, violating constitutional rights. Federal courts treat such removals as seizures under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments, actionable via §1983.
federal_fail_nodes.authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — limits removals to lawful emergencies and requires judicial review  
- **U.S. Constitution (4th & 14th Amendments)** — protects family integrity; requires due process
federal_fail_nodes.failure_basis: Child seized absent imminent danger or warrant; later found unconstitutional or unjustified.
federal_fail_nodes.corrective_hooks: §1983 civil action; injunctive relief; damages; federal monitoring under CFSR safety indicators.

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that a social worker and police officer who coerced entry into a home and directed a strip search of a child, without a warrant, consent, or exigency, violated clearly established Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights.
key_cases.relevance: Calabretta is the leading circuit authority that coerced warrantless entry by child protection workers is an actionable constitutional violation.
key_cases.quote: Under White, appellants' claim, that "a search warrant is not required for home investigatory visits by social workers," is simply not the law

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that officials may seize a child without prior judicial authorization only on reasonable cause to believe the child faces imminent danger of serious bodily injury, that reasonable investigative avenues must first be pursued, and that subjecting seized children to invasive medical examinations without parental notice implicated the family's constitutional rights.
key_cases.relevance: Seizing children on a nonexistent court order, without verification, is an unlawful removal under the Fourth Amendment.
key_cases.quote: the police cannot seize children suspected of being abused or neglected unless reasonable avenues of investigation are first pursued

key_cases.case_name: Rogers v. County of San Joaquin
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court reversed the grant of qualified immunity, holding that chronic medical neglect and unsanitary home conditions did not establish exigency and that the warrantless removal violated clearly established Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights.
key_cases.relevance: Rogers holds warrantless removal absent exigency to be an unlawful removal for which qualified immunity is unavailable.
key_cases.quote: we hold that it was clearly established that warrantless removal of children is permissible only in cases of exigency

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that removing a child from school for an examination on an emergency basis is unconstitutional where officials had reasonable time to seek judicial authorization consistent with the child's safety, though the defendants there received qualified immunity because the right was not clearly established in 1990.
key_cases.relevance: Tenenbaum is the Second Circuit's controlling statement that avoidable warrantless removals are unlawful.
key_cases.quote: it is unconstitutional for state officials to effect a child's removal on an "emergency" basis where there is reasonable time safely to obtain judicial authorization consistent with the child's safety

key_cases.case_name: Gates v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that the Fourth Amendment governs social workers' civil investigations, that the government may not seize a child from his parents absent a court order, parental consent, or exigent circumstances, and that removing a child from public school for a central-location interview requires a court order or a reasonable belief of abuse.
key_cases.relevance: Gates is the Fifth Circuit's controlling statement that seizure of a child without order, consent, or exigency is unlawful.
key_cases.quote: it is well established in this circuit that the Fourth Amendment regulates social workers' civil investigations

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that social workers' warrantless entry and removal of a child violated the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments where no exigency existed and no special needs exception applied, while remanding on whether reliance on the state statute made the officials' conduct objectively reasonable.
key_cases.relevance: Roska forecloses the special needs rationale that agencies commonly offer to justify warrantless removals.
key_cases.quote: We find no special need that renders the warrant requirement impracticable when social workers enter a home to remove a child, absent exigent circumstances

federal_fail_nodes.summary_html: A **state agency fails** to meet federal child-welfare performance standards, triggering **funding penalties** or corrective action under the CFSR or Single Audit Act.
federal_fail_nodes.authority_html:
- **Child & Family Services Reviews (45 CFR Part 1355)** — performance oversight and penalties  
- **Single Audit Act (31 U.S.C. §§ 7501–7507)** — audit of federally funded programs  
- **Inspector General Act (5 U.S.C. App.)** — oversight authority for HHS/OIG
federal_fail_nodes.failure_basis: Federal review finds systemic noncompliance with safety, permanency, or well-being metrics.
federal_fail_nodes.corrective_hooks: Program Improvement Plan (PIP); loss of IV-E reimbursement; OIG monitoring.
source_reference: CFSR, Single Audit Act, and IG Act links

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's 'reasonable efforts' requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), creates no right enforceable by beneficiaries through § 1983 or an implied right of action.
key_cases.relevance: Suter defines the remedy for federal compliance failure as withholding or corrective action by HHS rather than private suit.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that FERPA's nondisclosure provisions create no personal rights enforceable under § 1983, and that nothing short of an unambiguously conferred right will support a § 1983 action to enforce a federal spending statute.
key_cases.relevance: Gonzaga confirms that federal compliance failures are addressed through the funding agency, not through beneficiary § 1983 suits.
key_cases.quote: We now reject the notion that our cases permit anything short of an unambiguously conferred right to support a cause of action brought under § 1983

key_cases.case_name: Armstrong v. Exceptional Child Center, Inc.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Supremacy Clause creates no private cause of action and that Medicaid providers could not sue in equity to enforce a Spending Clause requirement whose sole remedy Congress vested in the Secretary.
key_cases.relevance: Armstrong confirms that the designed remedy for a state's failure to comply with federal child welfare conditions is administrative funding action.
key_cases.quote: To say that the Supremacy Clause does not confer a right of action is not to diminish the significant role that courts play in assuring the supremacy of federal law

key_cases.case_name: Health and Hospital Corporation of Marion Cty. v. Talevski
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed, holding that the Federal Nursing Home Reform Act's chemical-restraint and pre-transfer-notice provisions unambiguously confer individual rights presumptively enforceable under § 1983, and that the Act's remedial scheme was not comprehensive enough to rebut that presumption; the Court declined to disturb the Spending Clause § 1983 line running from Suter and Gonzaga.
key_cases.relevance: Talevski confirms that a systemwide performance duty owed to the funding agency is not privately actionable, while an individual-focused mandate may be, so compliance failures must be sorted provision by provision.
key_cases.quote: our precedent sets a demanding bar: Statutory provisions must unambiguously confer individual federal rights

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: A unanimous Court held that Title IV-D's requirement that a State's child support program be in 'substantial compliance' with federal law confers no individual right enforceable under § 1983, because it is a systemwide performance yardstick for the Secretary, and remanded for the lower courts to identify with particularity which specific statutory provisions, if any, create rights.
key_cases.relevance: Blessing supplies the three-factor framework - intent to benefit the plaintiff, a right not vague and amorphous, and a binding obligation on the State - by which any claimed federal compliance right must be tested provision by provision.
key_cases.quote: In order to seek redress through § 1983, however, a plaintiff must assert the violation of a federal right, not merely a violation of federal law

federal_fail_nodes.failure_name: Child Fatality / Serious Injury Under Supervision
federal_fail_nodes.summary_html: A child dies or suffers serious harm while **under agency supervision**, constituting systemic failure. Federal law mandates disclosure and review to identify causes and reforms.
federal_fail_nodes.authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — federal commission and review requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure of child-fatality cases
federal_fail_nodes.failure_basis: Fatality or serious injury occurs after agency involvement or placement; oversight failures identified.
federal_fail_nodes.corrective_hooks: Mandatory CAPTA review; publication of findings; policy revisions; federal/state corrective plans.
source_reference: Protect Our Kids Act and CAPTA fatality review mandates

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a state child protection agency to protect a child from private violence, even where the agency knew of the danger, absent a custodial relationship created by the State.
key_cases.relevance: Liability for a death under agency supervision turns on whether the State's custody created the DeShaney exception, not on the agency's knowledge alone.
key_cases.quote: As a general matter, then, we conclude that a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that officials may seize a child without prior judicial authorization only on reasonable cause to believe the child faces imminent danger of serious bodily injury, that reasonable investigative avenues must first be pursued, and that subjecting seized children to invasive medical examinations without parental notice implicated the family's constitutional rights.
key_cases.relevance: Harm inflicted on children after the State assumes custody falls outside DeShaney's no-duty rule and is actionable.
key_cases.quote: the police cannot seize children suspected of being abused or neglected unless reasonable avenues of investigation are first pursued

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a person involuntarily committed to state custody retains substantive due process liberty interests in reasonably safe conditions, freedom from undue bodily restraint, and such minimally adequate training as is reasonable to secure those interests, and that a qualified professional's judgment on how to meet them is presumptively valid; it vacated and remanded for application of that standard.
key_cases.relevance: Youngberg is the affirmative half of the analysis when a child is harmed under agency supervision: state custody creates the duty that DeShaney says private custody does not.
key_cases.quote: The State also has the unquestioned duty to provide reasonable safety for all residents and personnel within the institution

federal_fail_nodes.summary_html: Agency or actor engages in **discriminatory or retaliatory action**, violating civil-rights or placement-equality provisions. Federal statutes prohibit race, religion, sex, or disability bias in placements or investigations.
federal_fail_nodes.authority_html:
- **Multiethnic Placement Act (MEPA) & Interethnic Adoption Provisions (IEP)** — prohibits race/ethnicity discrimination in placements  
- **Civil Rights Act (42 U.S.C. § 2000d)** — Title VI discrimination prohibitions in federally funded programs
federal_fail_nodes.failure_basis: Placement, investigation, or service allocation influenced by impermissible bias or retaliation.
federal_fail_nodes.corrective_hooks: OIG/DOJ civil-rights investigation; corrective action plans; possible funding suspension.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court rejected every challenge to ICWA, upholding it against Article I and anticommandeering attacks on the merits and dismissing the equal protection and nondelegation challenges for lack of standing.
key_cases.relevance: Equal protection attacks on ICWA's classifications were dismissed for want of standing, so those claims remain unresolved rather than rejected on the merits.
key_cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that ICWA § 1912(f) does not bar termination where the Indian parent never had custody, and that § 1912(d)'s remedial-efforts requirement applies only where termination would precipitate the breakup of an existing Indian family.
key_cases.relevance: Adoptive Couple constrains ICWA-based claims of placement discrimination by tying the statute's protections to actual custodial relationships.
key_cases.quote: we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family's “breakup” would be precipitated by the termination of the parent's rights

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that caseworkers violated the Fourth Amendment by entering a private school and seizing a student for a custodial interview without a warrant, consent, or probable cause, and violated the parents' right to familial relations, although qualified immunity shielded them from damages.
key_cases.relevance: Doe v. Heck arose from an investigation triggered by a religious school's disciplinary practice and cabins investigation of families on that basis.
key_cases.quote: although child welfare caseworkers may investigate allegations of child abuse without violating parents' constitutional right to familial relations, they may not do so arbitrarily

key_cases.court: Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that a social worker and police officer who coerced entry into a home and directed a strip search of a child, without a warrant, consent, or exigency, violated clearly established Fourth and Fourteenth Amendment rights.
key_cases.relevance: The court rejected reliance on the family's religiosity and home schooling as a basis for intrusive investigation.
key_cases.quote: Under White, appellants' claim, that "a search warrant is not required for home investigatory visits by social workers," is simply not the law

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court reversed a custody modification that moved a child from her mother to her father solely because the mother had remarried a Black man, holding that the anticipated effects of private racial prejudice cannot justify a race-based custody decision under the Equal Protection Clause.
key_cases.relevance: Palmore is the one unambiguous Supreme Court holding that racial classification in the placement of a child is subject to the most exacting scrutiny and cannot be justified by private bias.
key_cases.quote: Private biases may be outside the reach of the law, but the law cannot, directly or indirectly, give them effect

federal_fail_nodes.summary_html: Agency fails to **disclose required data or reports**, obstructing transparency. Federal statutes require public reporting under CAPTA, FOIA, and Sunshine provisions.
federal_fail_nodes.authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — mandates public availability of child-fatality information  
- **Freedom of Information Act (5 U.S.C. § 552)** — public access to federal records  
- **Government in the Sunshine Act (5 U.S.C. § 552b)** — open-meeting requirements
federal_fail_nodes.failure_basis: Agency or contractor conceals data or obstructs mandated transparency reporting.
federal_fail_nodes.corrective_hooks: FOIA enforcement; federal audit; CAPTA compliance plan; possible funding sanctions.
source_reference: CAPTA, FOIA, and Sunshine Act transparency rules

key_cases.relevance: Gonzaga is the controlling authority that federal confidentiality and disclosure statutes generally confer no privately enforceable right.
key_cases.quote: We now reject the notion that our cases permit anything short of an unambiguously conferred right to support a cause of action brought under § 1983

key_cases.case_name: Armstrong v. Exceptional Child Center, Inc.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Supremacy Clause creates no private cause of action and that Medicaid providers could not sue in equity to enforce a Spending Clause requirement whose sole remedy Congress vested in the Secretary.
key_cases.relevance: Statutory disclosure duties tied to federal funding cannot be enforced through a Supremacy Clause action.
key_cases.quote: To say that the Supremacy Clause does not confer a right of action is not to diminish the significant role that courts play in assuring the supremacy of federal law

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's 'reasonable efforts' requirement, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), creates no right enforceable by beneficiaries through § 1983 or an implied right of action.
key_cases.relevance: Disclosure and plan obligations imposed on states as funding conditions are enforced by the Secretary, not by beneficiaries.
key_cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents

key_cases.case_name: M. L. B. v. S. L. J.
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a State may not condition an indigent parent's appeal from a decree terminating parental rights on her ability to prepay record preparation fees.
key_cases.relevance: Withholding the case record that a parent needs to seek review is itself a constitutionally cognizable transparency failure.
key_cases.quote: Mississippi may not deny M. L. B., because of her poverty, appellate review of the sufficiency of the evidence on which the trial court found her unfit to remain a parent

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: In a suit by parents exonerated of child abuse who remained listed on California's Child Abuse Central Index with no procedure to contest inclusion, the Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and held that Monell's policy-or-custom requirement applies to § 1983 claims against a municipality whether the relief sought is damages or prospective.
key_cases.relevance: A parent seeking prospective relief to correct or clear a maintained child abuse record must trace the failure to a municipal policy or custom, not merely to the acts of individual employees.
key_cases.quote: Nothing in the text of §1983 suggests that the causation requirement contained in the statute should change with the form of relief sought

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that a defendant charged with child abuse is entitled to have the confidential child-protective-services file reviewed in camera by the trial court for information material to his defense, but has no right to search the file himself or through counsel, and affirmed in part and reversed in part the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's broader disclosure order.
key_cases.relevance: Ritchie holds that a statutory confidentiality regime does not shield CPS files from all eyes, so a refusal to submit records for in camera judicial review is a cognizable disclosure failure.
key_cases.quote: Ritchie is entitled to have the CYS file reviewed by the trial court to determine whether it contains information that probably would have changed the outcome of his trial
